title: The eagle
intro: Naser Khosrow (1004–about 1088) was a government official in Merv until, at forty, a dream told him to give up wine and look for wisdom. He set out on a seven-year journey to Mecca and Cairo, described in his *Safarnameh* ('Travelogue'), and came home a missionary of the Ismaili Fatimid caliphs. Persecuted for his faith, he spent his last years in exile in the valley of Yamgan, in the mountains of Badakhshan, writing stern, intelligent poems about wisdom and the soul. This short poem is the best known of them: a proud eagle boasts that the whole world lies beneath its wings, until an arrow fletched with eagle feathers brings it down. Its last words have become a proverb.

lines.fa: روزی ز سر سنگ عقابی به هوا خاست / وندر طلب طعمه پر و بال بیاراست
lines.r: ruzi ze sar-e sang 'oghābi be havā khāst / vandar talab-e to'me par o bāl biyārāst
lines.en: One day an eagle rose into the air from the top of a rock, / and spread out its wings and feathers in search of prey.
lines.faV: روزی ز سَرِ سَنگ عُقابی به هَوا خاست / وَندَر طَلَبِ طُعمه پَر و بال بیاراست

lines.fa: بر راستی بال نظر کرد و چنین گفت / امروز همه روی جهان زیر پر ماست
lines.r: bar rāsti-ye bāl nazar kard o chonin goft / emruz hame ru-ye jahān zir-e par-e māst
lines.en: It looked at how straight its wings were, and said: / 'Today the whole face of the world lies under my wings.
words: is ours – ما + است (the eagle says 'we')
lines.faV: بَر راستیِ بال نَظَر کَرد و چُنین گُفت / اِمروز هَمه رویِ جَهان زیرِ پَرِ ماست

lines.fa: بر اوج چو پرواز کنم از نظر تیز / می‌بینم اگر ذره‌ای اندر ته دریاست
lines.r: bar owj cho parvāz konam az nazar-e tiz / mi-binam agar zarre-i andar tah-e daryāst
lines.en: When I fly up to the heights, my sharp eyes / can see a speck of dust at the bottom of the sea.
lines.note: Some editions read «تک دریاست» *tak-e daryāst*, with the same meaning.
words: in – the old form of در
lines.faV: بَر اَوج چو پَرواز کُنَم اَز نَظَرِ تیز / می‌بینَم اَگَر ذَرّه‌ای اَندَر تَهِ دَریاست

lines.fa: گر بر سر خاشاک یکی پشه بجنبد / جنبیدن آن پشه عیان در نظر ماست
lines.r: gar bar sar-e khāshāk yeki pashe bejonbad / jonbidan-e ān pashe 'ayān dar nazar-e māst
lines.en: If a gnat stirs on a blade of straw, / I can see that gnat's stirring plainly.'
lines.faV: گَر بَر سَرِ خاشاک یِکی پَشه بِجُنبَد / جُنبیدَنِ آن پَشه عَیان دَر نَظَرِ ماست

lines.fa: بسیار منی کرد و ز تقدیر نترسید / بنگر که از این چرخ جفاپیشه چه برخاست
lines.r: besyār mani kard o ze taghdir natarsid / bengar ke az in charkh-e jafā-pishe che barkhāst
lines.en: It boasted a great deal and did not fear fate – / now see what came of this cruel turning sky.
words: to boast, to be full of oneself (من 'I' + ـی)
to rise; to come of, to result
lines.faV: بِسیار مَنی کَرد و ز تَقدیر نَتَرسید / بِنگَر که اَز این چَرخِ جَفاپیشه چه بَرخاست

lines.fa: ناگه ز کمینگاه یکی سخت کمانی / تیری ز قضا و قدر انداخت بر او راست
lines.r: nāgah ze kamingāh yeki sakht kamāni / tiri ze ghazā vo ghadar andākht bar u rāst
lines.en: Suddenly, from his hiding place, an archer with a strong bow / shot an arrow of fate straight at it.
words: with a strong bow – a strong archer
lines.faV: ناگَه ز کَمینگاه یِکی سَخت کَمانی / تیری ز قَضا و قَدَر اَنداخت بَر او راست

lines.fa: بر بال عقاب آمد آن تیر جگردوز / وز ابر مر او را به سوی خاک فروکاست
lines.r: bar bāl-e 'oghāb āmad ān tir-e jegar-duz / vaz abr mar u rā be su-ye khāk forukāst
lines.en: That piercing arrow struck the eagle's wing / and brought it down from the clouds to the earth.
words: liver-piercing – deadly (جگر 'liver', the seat of feeling)
it (as object) – مر … را is an old way of marking the object
lines.faV: بَر بالِ عُقاب آمَد آن تیرِ جِگَردوز / وَز اَبر مَر او را به سویِ خاک فُروکاست

lines.fa: بر خاک بیفتاد و بغلتید چو ماهی / وانگاه پر خویش گشاد از چپ و از راست
lines.r: bar khāk biyoftād o beghaltid cho māhi / vāngāh par-e khish goshād az chap o az rāst
lines.en: It fell to the ground and flapped about like a fish, / and then spread its wings to the left and to the right.
lines.faV: بَر خاک بیُفتاد و بِغَلتید چو ماهی / وانگاه پَرِ خویش گُشاد اَز چَپ و اَز راست

lines.fa: گفتا عجب است این که ز چوبی و ز آهن / این تیزی و تندی و پریدن ز کجا خاست
lines.r: goftā 'ajab ast in ke ze chubi vo ze āhan / in tizi vo tondi vo paridan ze kojā khāst
lines.en: It said: 'How strange – a piece of wood and a bit of iron: / where did they get this sharpness, this speed, this flight?'
words: he said – گفت, with ـا added for the metre
lines.faV: گُفتا عَجَب اَست این که ز چوبی و ز آهَن / این تیزی و تُندی و پَریدَن ز کُجا خاست

lines.fa: چون نیک نظر کرد پر خویش در او دید / گفتا ز که نالیم که از ماست که بر ماست
lines.r: chon nik nazar kard par-e khish dar u did / goftā ze ke nālim ke az māst ke bar māst
lines.en: When it looked closely, it saw its own feathers on the arrow. / It said: 'Whom can we blame? What has struck us came from us.'
lines.note: Some editions read the first half «زی تیر نگه کرد و پر خویش بر او دید» 'it looked at the arrow and saw its own feathers on it'.
words: is upon us, falls on us
lines.faV: چون نیک نَظَر کَرد پَرِ خویش دَر او دید / گُفتا ز که نالیم که اَز ماست که بَر ماست

commentary:
**The story.** It is a fable, told in ten quick couplets. The eagle has everything: height, speed, eyes that can see a gnat move on a straw. Its fault is [[منی|mani]] – 'I-ness', pride – and its pride makes it forget fate. The arrow comes from nowhere, from a hidden archer, and the fallen eagle is puzzled: how can a stick of wood and a bit of iron fly so fast? Then it sees the answer: the arrow is fletched with eagle feathers. Aesop tells the same fable ('The Eagle and the Arrow'); Naser Khosrow gives it a sharper moral. Our worst wounds are made with our own feathers: what we suffer, we have usually brought on ourselves.

**The rhythm.** The metre is a long, heavy *hazaj*, *DUM-DUM-da da-DUM-DUM-da da-DUM-DUM-da da-DUM-DUM*, which suits a story that swoops and falls: *ru-zi ze sa-re san-ge 'o-ghā-bi be ha-vā khāst*. All the couplets rhyme on [[ـاست|-āst]] – [[خاست|khāst]], [[بیاراست|biyārāst]], [[ماست|māst]], [[دریاست|daryāst]], [[برخاست|barkhāst]], [[راست|rāst]], [[فروکاست|forukāst]] – and the last line rhymes twice, [[از ماست که بر ماست|az māst ke bar māst]], to drive the point home.

**The grammar.** The poem is full of the prefix [[ب|be-]] on past verbs, which modern Persian has dropped: [[بیاراست|biyārāst]] 'arranged', [[بیفتاد|biyoftād]] 'fell', [[بغلتید|beghaltid]] 'rolled'. [[گفتا|goftā]] is simply [[گفت|goft]] with an extra [[ا|-ā]] for the metre, [[وندر|vandar]] is [[و اندر|va andar]] 'and in', and [[مر او را|mar u rā]] is an old way of saying [[او را|u rā]]. The last couplet in modern prose: [[وقتی خوب نگاه کرد، پر خودش را روی تیر دید و گفت: از چه کسی شکایت کنیم؟ هر چه بر سر ما می‌آید از خود ماست|vaghti khub negāh kard, par-e khod-ash rā ru-ye tir did va goft: az che kasi shekāyat konim? har che bar sar-e mā mi-āyad az khod-e māst]].

**Using it.** [[از ماست که بر ماست|az māst ke bar māst]] is one of the commonest proverbs in Persian. Iranians say it about a country's troubles, a team's defeat, a family quarrel – any time the blame lies at home. Many people learned the whole poem at school and can still recite it from the first line to the last.
